extracted.intended_audience: British political class, parliamentarians, and the educated public concerned with governance
extracted.subtask_description: A rhetorical and argumentative essay addressing proper constitution, administration, and dangers of court favoritism; argues principles for choosing ministers and structuring government institutions. Intended to persuade legislators and the politically engaged public about sound polity and the risks of factional court influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise of discretionary powers on public principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The discretionary powers which are necessarily vested in the monarch ... should all be exercised upon public principles and national grounds, and not on the likings or prejudices, the intrigues or policies, of a court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke argues that discretionary powers (nomination to office, conduct of peace and war, ordering the revenue, execution of laws) must be used for public good rather than private favor; otherwise the spirit of the constitution is undermined even if the letter of law is not violated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration correspondent to the legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: Every sort of government ought to have its administration correspondent to its legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If administration does not reflect the character and will of the legislature (and thereby the people), disorder and a breakdown of constitutional checks will follow. The composition of the executive must align with the representative/elective element of the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of ministers acceptable to the people
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament ought to refuse to support government until power was in the hands of persons who were acceptable to the people, or while factions predominated in the court in which the nation had no confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke treats parliamentary refusal to support an unacceptable administration as a key mechanism ensuring ministers are trustworthy and have public confidence; appointing ministers without such acceptability is a grave constitutional defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventive design of institutions to exclude bad men
rubrics_metrics.description: Every good political institution must have a preventive operation as well as a remedial. It ought to have a natural tendency to exclude bad men from government, and not to trust for the safety of the state to subsequent punishment alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should be constructed so they make it difficult for unfit persons to gain power; relying only on later punishment is inadequate because punishment is often tardy and uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public estimation as pledge of fitness for office
rubrics_metrics.description: Before men are put forward into the great trusts of the state, they ought by their conduct to have obtained such a degree of estimation in their country, as may be some sort of pledge and security to the public, that they will not abuse those trusts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke emphasizes pre-existing reputation, conduct, and public esteem as qualifications and safeguards for appointment to high office; this functions as a practical test of trustworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of favoritism and a system of patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: It is this unnatural infusion of a system of favoritism into a government which in a great part of its constitution is popular, that has raised the present ferment in the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favoritism corrodes public administration by placing private attachments above national grounds; Burke links favoritism to disorder, innovation, and general decay of government functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and opposition to clandestine 'back-stairs' government
rubrics_metrics.description: They make no complaints of the power of those peers who are always in the train of a court... If some peers set themselves against a back-stairs influence and clandestine government, then the alarm begins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secret patronage and influence-peddling (back-stairs government) are dangerous; public, visible channels of appointment and influence are required to maintain constitutional balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid separating the court from the administration
rubrics_metrics.description: There first appeared the idea of separating the court from the administration; of carrying everything from national connection to personal regards; and of forming a regular party for that purpose, under the name of king's men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke condemns a deliberate separation that substitutes personal regard and court factionalism for national, party-based administration; such separation creates a 'king's men' clique harmful to the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist schemes that weaken executory power to aggrandize the court
rubrics_metrics.description: The plan proceeds expressly on the idea of enfeebling the regular executory power. It proceeds on the idea of weakening the state in order to strengthen the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies that intentionally weaken the functioning executive (to make the court appear more important) are self-defeating and dangerous; sound policy protects effective execution of laws and state functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions should preserve both negative and positive public controls
rubrics_metrics.description: One great end ... is that the prince shall not be able to violate the laws. This is useful indeed and fundamental. But ... it is next in order, and equal in importance, that the discretionary powers ... should all be exercised upon public principles and national grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal restraints on the monarch are necessary but insufficient; active, principle-based exercise of discretion by the executive and ministers is equally important to preserve a living constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of office should avoid creating insulated, life-tenured sinecures
rubrics_metrics.description: The members of the court faction are fully indemnified for not holding places on the slippery heights ... Their places are in express legal tenure, or, in effect, all of them for life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permanent, insulated positions occupied by court clients create a secure base of patronage that prevents ministers from reorganizing administration and undermines meritocratic control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding deliberate disunion and sowing jealousies among orders
rubrics_metrics.description: All this is done upon their favorite principle of disunion, of sowing jealousies amongst the different orders of the state, and of disjointing the natural strength of the kingdom; that it may be rendered incapable of resisting the sinister designs of wicked men, who have engrossed the royal power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining unity among social and political orders is a protective measure; deliberate disunion is a tactic of faction to prevent effective opposition and good governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of intermediaries and divided administrations as a danger sign
rubrics_metrics.description: The cabal have established a sort of rota in the court. All sorts of parties, by this means, have been brought into administration; from whence few have had the good fortune to escape without disgrace; none at all without considerable losses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rotating or deliberately fragmented administrations that keep ministers weak and dependent are indicators of manipulative faction; stable, coherent administrations better serve public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary duty to check and refuse support to corrupt or factional administrations
rubrics_metrics.description: If Parliament will tamely see evil men take possession of all the strongholds of their country ... such a Parliament will give countenance to their measures also.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke assigns to Parliament an active duty: to refuse support to administrations composed of persons lacking public confidence, thereby preventing the consolidation of factional power.
